title: RSI: what 'overbought' really means
body:
RSI(14) compares average gains to average losses over 14 sessions and maps it to 0-100. Above 70 is conventionally 'overbought', below 30 'oversold'.

The common mistake: treating RSI > 70 as a sell signal. In a strong trend RSI can sit above 70 for weeks — that is what strength looks like. RSI is most useful as a *divergence* tool: price makes a new high, RSI makes a lower high, and the move is running out of fuel.

Use it with trend context. RSI 75 in a stock above its rising 200-DMA means momentum. RSI 75 in a downtrending stock usually means a bear-market rally.

title: Why volume confirms (or kills) a move
body:
Price tells you what happened. Volume tells you how many people agreed.

A 4% rally on 3x average volume means real institutional buying — size had to be absorbed. The same 4% on half-average volume means a thin book moved easily and can just as easily reverse.

This dashboard reports volume as a z-score vs the 20-day average, so +2.5 means 'today's volume is 2.5 standard deviations above normal'. Anything past +2 is worth a look. Breakouts without volume fail disproportionately often.

title: Moving averages: 50-DMA and 200-DMA
body:
The 50-day moving average is the medium-term trend; the 200-day is the long-term one. Their relationship is the cheapest regime filter that exists.

Price > 50-DMA > 200-DMA = uptrend, buy dips. Price < 50-DMA < 200-DMA = downtrend, rallies get sold. 50 crossing above 200 is a 'golden cross'; below is a 'death cross'. Both are *lagging* — they confirm a trend that already started, they do not predict one.

Their real value is as a stop-thinking filter: do not buy breakouts in stocks below their 200-DMA.

title: Gap ups and gap downs
body:
A gap is when today's open is away from yesterday's close — news arrived while the market was shut.

Three kinds matter. A *breakaway gap* starts a new trend out of a range, usually on heavy volume, and tends to hold. A *continuation gap* appears mid-trend and confirms it. An *exhaustion gap* comes after an extended run and marks the end.

The tell is what happens after the first hour. If a gap up holds above the opening price all day, buyers are in control. If it fills (price returns to yesterday's close), the news was already priced in.

title: How news sentiment is scored here
body:
Headlines are scored -1 to +1. The base scorer is VADER with a finance lexicon layered on, because general-purpose sentiment models read 'beat', 'miss', 'downgrade' and 'cut' as neutral words.

Scores are aggregated with a 3-day half-life, so a headline from today counts roughly twice as much as one from three days ago.

Two cautions. Sentiment measures *coverage tone*, not truth — a stock can rally on bad news if the news was less bad than feared. And headline sentiment is largely already in the price by the time you read it. Treat it as context, not a signal.

title: ATR: sizing positions by volatility
body:
Average True Range measures how far a stock typically travels in a day, including gaps. Shown here as a percentage of price.

Its main use is position sizing. If you risk 1% of capital per trade and the stock's ATR is 3%, a stop placed 1.5 ATR away is 4.5% — so your position can be at most ~22% of capital. A 1% ATR stock lets you take a much bigger position for the same risk.

Sizing every position the same rupee amount, regardless of volatility, is one of the most common ways retail accounts blow up.

title: Market breadth: is the rally real?
body:
Breadth is how many stocks participate. An index can rise while most of its constituents fall, if the few largest weights are up.

Two measures here: percent of tracked stocks advancing today, and percent trading above their own 50-DMA. Above 60% on the second is a healthy, broad trend. Below 35% while the index is near highs is a narrow rally — historically fragile.

Breadth deteriorating while the index makes new highs is one of the few genuinely useful leading warnings.

title: Reading this dashboard's probability honestly
body:
The percentage on the Model tab is the probability a stock OUTPERFORMS the median stock in the universe over the horizon. It is relative strength, not direction.

That distinction is the whole design. An absolute 'will it go up' target was tried first and scored AUC 0.49 on holdout -- worse than a coin flip -- because most of a stock's short-term return is the market's return, and no technical indicator predicts that. Removing the cross-sectional median strips the market factor out and leaves the part these features can actually speak to.

So 60% does not mean the stock rises. In a falling market the top-ranked stock usually still falls, just less than its peers. If you want a view on market direction, look at the regime and breadth on the Overview tab, not at this number.

AUC 0.50 is a coin flip; realistic cross-sectional equity models land at 0.52-0.56, and so does this one. That edge is real but small, shows up only across many independent positions, and is erased by overtrading. The Live scorecard grades every matured prediction against what actually happened -- trust that over the training metric.

title: Sector rotation
body:
Money moves between sectors in fairly persistent cycles. Early recovery favours financials and cyclicals; late cycle favours energy and materials; contraction favours staples, utilities and pharma.

The Sectors view ranks equal-weighted sector returns over 1, 5 and 20 days. What matters is the *change* in ranking, not the level. A sector moving from bottom quartile to top over two weeks, on rising volume, is rotation in progress.

Individual stocks inherit most of their return from their sector. Picking the right sector and an average stock usually beats picking the best stock in the wrong sector.

title: Position sizing and stop losses
body:
Decide the exit before the entry. Two rules survive contact with reality:

1. Risk a fixed small percentage of capital per position — 1% is a common choice. Position size = (capital x 1%) / (entry - stop).
2. Place the stop where your thesis is wrong, not where your pain threshold is. Below the recent swing low, or 1.5-2 ATR away.

Averaging down on a losing position without a pre-planned level is how a small loss becomes an unrecoverable one.
